market_context: United States/international; distinguishes opened canned tomato paste from resealable tubes and prioritizes manufacturer instructions.
title: How Long Does Opened Tomato Paste Last in the Fridge?

seo.title: How Long Does Opened Tomato Paste Last?
seo.meta_description: Canned tomato paste is best used within about 5–7 refrigerated days, while resealable tubes may have longer label guidance. Learn how to store leftovers.
seo.search_intent: Know how long opened tomato paste lasts and why cans and resealable tubes can have different refrigerator lives.

excerpt: Tomato paste left in an opened can fits the 5–7 day high-acid canned-food range. Tubes are packaged differently, so follow their own after-opening instructions.
content_html:
Tomato paste from an opened can is best treated as a high-acid canned food and used within about 5–7 refrigerated days. A resealable tube is a different package and may carry a substantially longer after-opening instruction, so the label on the tube should control.

That distinction explains why two people can give very different answers and both be describing products called “tomato paste.” A small metal can exposes the whole remaining surface at once; a capped tube is designed to dispense a little at a time with far less exposure.

An opened can follows the high-acid canned-food window

USDA guidance gives high-acid canned foods, including tomato products, roughly five to seven days in the refrigerator after opening. Keep the paste at 40°F (4°C) or colder and cover it promptly.

It is safe to refrigerate an opened can, but tomato paste is especially prone to drying, darkening, and picking up refrigerator odors on its exposed surface. Scraping the remainder into a small clean covered container is usually a better quality choice. A smaller container also leaves less headspace and makes it easier to see the amount left.

Do not add fresh garlic, herbs, or oil to the storage container in an attempt to “preserve” the paste unless you are following a tested recipe. Adding ingredients changes the product and can create a different safety situation rather than extending its life.

Tubes can legitimately have a different after-opening life

Tomato paste sold in a squeezable metal or plastic tube is packaged for repeated small uses. The cap limits exposure and the formulation and processing may differ from canned paste. Manufacturers therefore sometimes give a much longer refrigerated after-opening period.

There is no reason to ignore a package-specific instruction and force a tube into the five-to-seven-day can rule. Read the label, keep the cap and threads clean, close it tightly, and refrigerate it if instructed.

Conversely, do not take the long life printed on one tube and apply it to an opened can from another manufacturer. The package design is part of the storage guidance. “Tomato paste” describes the ingredient, not an identical post-opening storage system.

Freezing spoonfuls is the easiest solution for leftover cans

Because recipes often use only one or two tablespoons, tomato paste is an ideal food to freeze in tiny portions. Drop measured spoonfuls onto a lined tray, freeze until firm, then transfer them to a freezer container or bag. A silicone ice-cube tray also works.

Once frozen, a tablespoon can go directly into many hot sauces, braises, soups, and stews. The texture change from freezing is essentially irrelevant because the paste will dissolve into the dish.

Freeze the portions while the paste is fresh, not after it has sat forgotten for a week. Label the container so red frozen cubes are not mistaken for another sauce. This approach eliminates the pressure to use an entire small can within a few days.

Another useful habit is to flatten the surface before covering canned paste. Reducing exposed ridges does not make the food sterile, but it limits drying and makes later changes easier to notice. Use a clean spoon each time rather than double-dipping a utensil that has touched meat, cheese, or another ingredient.

Darkening can be quality loss, but mold means discard

The exposed surface of tomato paste can darken as it oxidizes and dries. Mild darkening alone is not the same thing as visible mold, although it signals declining quality. If you see mold, fuzzy growth, unusual bubbling, or smell a clearly fermented or rotten odor, discard the paste.

Do not simply scrape mold off a soft, moist food and use what remains. Nor should you taste a questionable paste to test it. If the package is swollen, leaking, or damaged before opening, that is a separate reason for caution.

For planning purposes, the answer is: opened canned tomato paste, about 5–7 refrigerated days; tomato paste in a resealable tube, follow the manufacturer’s after-opening instruction. For a half-used can, freezing tablespoon portions on day one is often the most practical choice.

faq.question: How long does canned tomato paste last after opening?
faq.answer: About 5–7 days refrigerated is a useful USDA high-acid canned-food guideline.

faq.question: Does tomato paste in a tube last longer?
faq.answer: It often can because the package is designed for repeated dispensing. Follow the specific after-opening instruction on the tube.

faq.question: Can tomato paste be frozen?
faq.answer: Yes. Freezing measured tablespoon portions is one of the easiest ways to avoid wasting an opened can.
